# Digest E — Mic 4–5b (5:2–15 + Excursus: Mic 4–5 as Compilation)

Attributed throughout to [[james-nogalski|James D. Nogalski]], *The Book of Micah* (NICOT), unless marked as Nogalski citing another scholar. Primary-text claims of [[micah|Micah]] are attributed to the biblical text as Nogalski presents it.

---

### C-E-01 — Mic 5:1 as bridge; king theme into 5:2–4
- **Locus:** local 1–3 ≈ raw 3241–3243
- **Quote:** “Micah 5:1 (4:14) also serves as a bridge text to the final you saying (5:2–4[1–3]) that begins in the next verse and concludes the second group of sayings that structures chapters 4–5. The end of 5:1 (4:14) introduces the theme of the role of the king, a topic that continues in 5:2–4(1–3).”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:1(4:14) bridges into the final “you” saying of the second group in Mic 4–5 and opens the king/ruler theme continued in 5:2–4.

### C-E-02 — Addressee shift: Lady Zion → Bethlehem (2ms “you”)
- **Locus:** local 10–11 ≈ raw 3250–3251
- **Quote:** “Micah 5:2(1) leaves behind the direct address of Lady Zion and its second-person feminine singular terms that identify Lady Zion as the primary addressee in 4:8b–5:1. Rather, 5:2 returns to the second-person masculine singular form of you that began the second group of sayings in 4:8.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:2 shifts from 2fs Lady Zion address (4:8b–5:1) back to 2ms “you,” identifying the addressee as Bethlehem and aligning with the 2ms frame that began at 4:8.

### C-E-03 — Bethlehem Ephrathah: Davidic hometown and clan
- **Locus:** local 12–14 ≈ raw 3252–3254
- **Quote:** “Bethlehem lies approximately six miles south of Jerusalem. It is famous as the hometown of David and the place where Samuel went at Yahweh’s command to anoint David as king (1 Sam 16:1, 4; cf. 17:12). Ephrathah appears to be considered a leading clan of Bethlehem, tracing its roots back to Caleb, according to genealogical material in Chronicles (1 Chr 2:19, 50). … One tradition even identifies Ephrathah as an earlier name for Bethlehem (Gen 35:19).”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Bethlehem is David’s hometown (~6 mi S of [[jerusalem|Jerusalem]]); Ephrathah is a leading Bethlehem clan (Caleb/Chronicles; Ruth; 1 Sam 17:12; Ps 132:6; Gen 35:19 as earlier name).

### C-E-04 — Two claims of 5:2: ruler from Bethlehem; origins from distant past
- **Locus:** local 15–16 ≈ raw 3255–3256
- **Quote:** “The last half of 5:2(1) makes two important claims: (1) that someone will go forth from Bethlehem to rule on Yahweh’s behalf, and (2) that this ruler’s origins go back to the distant past. … Despite the city’s seeming insignificance, Yahweh announces a new ruler will go forth from the city, and the announcement stresses both that he comes from Bethlehem and that Yahweh commissions him by putting two prepositional phrases side by side before the verb … : from you for me he will go forth.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Mic 5:2 claims (1) a Yahweh-commissioned ruler goes forth from Bethlehem and (2) his origins reach the distant past; emphasis is “from you for me he will go forth.”

### C-E-05 — Distant past = dynastic continuity of Davidic promise, not cessation
- **Locus:** local 17–18 ≈ raw 3257–3258
- **Quote:** “The reference to the distant past emphasizes the continuing hope for a Davidic ruler. Yahweh is the speaker, and significantly, Yahweh essentially affirms that this ancient promise has not ceased. The next ruler, like David, will come from Bethlehem and his origins go back into perpetuity. This phrasing links the future leader with the past in a way that can only imply a continuation of the Davidic promise that one of David’s descendants would sit on the throne into perpetuity (2 Sam 7:12–13).”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** “From of old / distant past / perpetuity” in 5:2 means dynastic continuity of the [[david|Davidic]] promise (2 Sam 7:12–13)—hope that the promise has not ceased—not a metaphysical preexistence doctrine in Nogalski’s OT-context reading.

### C-E-06 — Downplaying Jerusalem and “king”; Yahweh remains true king
- **Locus:** local 21–22 ≈ raw 3261–3262
- **Quote:** “Several commentators note, however, that the phrasing of this verse notably downplays two important elements of this royal promise. It avoids any reference to Jerusalem, and it does not refer to the future ruler as king. … By alluding to David’s origins as insignificant among the clans of Judah, the statement avoids any association with Jerusalem and the sins of its leaders. By avoiding naming this ruler ‘king,’ this phrasing avoids anything that gets in the way of remembering that Yahweh is king, not a human who only acts as his agent.”
- **Claim (Nogalski, reporting commentators [Wolff, Jeremias, Allen]):** 5:2 omits Jerusalem and the title “king,” distancing from past royal sin and stressing Yahweh as king with the human as agent—though Nogalski calls these “subtle connotations at best.”

### C-E-07 — Primary rhetorical aim: hope in continuity of Davidic leadership
- **Locus:** local 22–25 ≈ raw 3262–3265
- **Quote:** “The rhetorical aim of the passage primarily offers hope in the continuity of Davidic leadership for all Israelites. Yes, returning to Bethlehem avoids the association with the sins of past Davidic kings, but Yahweh still expects the ruler to go forth from there. Such subtle nuances would not change expectations that this new ruler would return to Jerusalem. … By announcing Yahweh has appointed a new ruler with Davidic lineage, Mic 5:2(1) taps into these hopes.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Main aim is hope for continuous Davidic leadership; Bethlehem origin does not cancel expectation of return to Jerusalem (2 Sam 7 house-of-David / house-of-Yahweh bond).

### C-E-08 — NT messianic use vs OT context (Matthew 2:5–6)
- **Locus:** local 26 ≈ raw 3266
- **Quote:** “Micah 5:2(1) serves as a source text in the Gospels to draw attention to the parallels between David and Jesus. Not only was Jesus a descendant of David, but like David, Jesus was also born in the small town of Bethlehem (see Matt 2:5–6). The wise men from the East and Herod are informed that the messiah’s birth in Bethlehem is foretold in Mic 5:2–3(1–2). While the New Testament writers treated the verse as a prognostication, modern scholars do not typically treat Mic 5:2 as a messianic prediction in its original context.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Gospels (Matt 2:5–6) treat Mic 5:2–3 as messianic prognostication linking Jesus and David via Bethlehem; modern critical scholarship typically does **not** read Mic 5:2 as messianic prediction in its original context—Nogalski’s OT/NT distinction.

### C-E-09 — Dating of 5:2 and content of the hope (Davidic restoration)
- **Locus:** local 26 ≈ raw 3266
- **Quote:** “Rather, Mic 5:2–3 refers to the hometown of David in the eleventh century BCE, three centuries before the eighth-century prophet Micah and likely another two to three centuries before this text was penned in the postexilic period. Specific dates for this text range from the sixth to the fourth centuries BCE. Micah 5:2 anticipates a new king from the Davidic line who will restore the kingdom of the sons of Israel as it was in the time of David and Solomon. Matthew and the other Gospel writers go to considerable lengths to make certain their readers see Jesus as a different kind of king, one who is not interested in political power.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** In OT context, 5:2 anticipates a new Davidic king restoring the kingdom as under David/Solomon; composition often dated postexilic (6th–4th c. BCE range); NT reworks kingship toward a non-political model.

### C-E-10 — “He will give them up”: subject is Yahweh, not the ruler
- **Locus:** local 28, 50–51 ≈ raw 3268, 3290–3291
- **Quote:** “The idea of sending the people of Judah into exile before bringing them back makes sense in the context of divine judgment, whereas associating such action with the king lacks motivation. Yahweh must therefore be assumed as the one surrendering them up. … Since 5:3(2) begins with therefore, the verse makes sense as a prophetic oracle that announces the decision of Yahweh to act. In this interpretation, Yahweh gives up the tribes of Judah (to their enemy) until the tribes will reunite and return to the land.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Subject of “give” in 5:3 is Yahweh (surrender/exile judgment), not the Bethlehem ruler; form (“therefore”) fits a prophetic decision-oracle of delayed promise.

### C-E-11 — Entities in 5:3: tribes, brothers, sons of Israel
- **Locus:** local 30, 52 ≈ raw 3270, 3292
- **Quote:** “The third-person masculine plural reference to them refers formally back to the tribes of Judah, which also appears to be the same group called his brothers in 5:3b(2b), the group who will return to the sons of Israel. … The destination, however, is not expressed in purely geographical terms. The ruler and his brothers will return to the sons of Israel. … The territory will extend beyond Judah to include the territory of all the sons of Israel.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** “Them” / “his brothers” = tribes of Judah related to the Bethlehem figure; return is to “sons of Israel” with familial-political force—reunified territory beyond Judah.

### C-E-12 — “One giving birth”: Isa 7:14 parallel tested and distinguished
- **Locus:** local 32–46 ≈ raw 3272–3286
- **Quote:** “Several commentators see 5:3(2) as an allusion to Isa 7:14 in light of the reference to the woman giving birth (Mic 4:9–10) and the coming ruler (Mic 5:2[1]). … The differences between the two passages are, however, significant. Isaiah 7:14 announces a sign, with the word ‘sign’ serving as the direct object of ‘give.’ … The verb give in Mic 5:3 has an attached pronominal suffix as direct object, but it uses the word ntn to mean ‘give up’ or ‘turn over.’ It announces punishment.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Lexical birth-language invites comparison with [[isaiah|Isa]] 7:14, but differences are decisive: Isaiah’s “give” has “sign” as object and hope-omen; Micah’s ntn = “give up/turn over” = punishment. Alternatives: imminence metaphor; dual function (pain of 4:9 + future ruler via Isa 7:14 / 9:5–6).

### C-E-13 — Delayed promise: exilic/postexilic anthology? Zerubbabel? Amos 9:11–12
- **Locus:** local 54–58 ≈ raw 3294–3298
- **Quote:** “Modern scholars frequently interpret this verse, and its context, as an oracle whose author speaks to an exilic or postexilic audience to offer hope for restoration of the Davidic monarchy following the destruction of 587 BCE. … One might see in 5:2–4(1–3) an oblique allusion to the hopes that certain parties had for the governorship of Zerubbabel … (see esp. Hag 2:20–23; Zech 4:6–10). The promise in Amos 9:11–12 … represents another particularly clear parallel to Mic 5:2–3 in that it articulates a hope for a reconstitution of the Davidic monarchy with a Judean king centered in Jerusalem.”
- **Claim (Nogalski, reporting scholarship):** Common reading: exilic/postexilic hope for Davidic restoration; possible oblique Zerubbabel link; Amos 9:11–12 as parallel “booth of David” hope—Judean vision of reunified kingdom including Davidic-Solomonic borders.

### C-E-14 — Problems with pure exilic relocation; Assyria vs Babylon; chronological markers
- **Locus:** local 60 ≈ raw 3300
- **Quote:** “Nevertheless, such a reading creates real dilemmas for at least two reasons. First … it forces the reader to assume a perspective that is not clearly signaled in the text by forcing the reader to relocate the reading of this text so that it reflects issues of concern for the late exilic or early postexilic period. Second, the assumption that 5:1(2) alludes to the role of Zerubbabel ignores the fact that such allusion is quite oblique. … the second-person masculine singular addressees of this larger unit (mentioned in 4:8; 5:2[1]) frame three sayings that all begin with now and seem to expect that the reader of these verses interpret them in light of the action of the book associated with an eighth-century prophet. … the third group of sayings in chapters 4–5 is characterized by the recurring use of and it will be (wəhāyâ) that appears four times (5:5[4], 7[6], 8[7], 10[9]) … At the same time, the enemy explicitly mentioned in 5:5(4) is Assyria, not Babylon … To be sure, Mic 4:10 mentions Babylon explicitly…”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Pure exilic/Zerubbabel readings under-signal in the text; framing 2ms + “now” orients to eighth-century prophetic book-time; third group uses future wəhāyâ; named enemy in 5:5 is Assyria (though 4:10 names Babylon).

### C-E-15 — Shepherd ruler in strength / pride of Yahweh’s name (5:4)
- **Locus:** local 62–64 ≈ raw 3302–3304
- **Quote:** “The statement that he will stand has a performative aspect … It presents the king as one who accepts a role of authority (cf. Isa 3:3). … The phrases ‘to shepherd in strength’ or ‘to shepherd in the strength of Yahweh’ do not appear elsewhere, but they draw upon the shepherd imagery portraying the king’s role as military commander leading the forces of Yahweh in the battle. … The verse also expects the royal figure to perform his role as shepherd in the pride of the name of Yahweh, a phrase that also appears nowhere else in the Old Testament. The word pride means splendor.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:4’s unique formulations portray the ruler as ideal righteous king: “stand” = accepting authority; shepherd in Yahweh’s strength = military-commander shepherd; “pride/splendor of the name of Yahweh” = behavior regulated by commitment to Yahweh.

### C-E-16 — Name theology; subordinate royal image; Deut 12 / Dtr presence
- **Locus:** local 64–66 ≈ raw 3304–3306
- **Quote:** “As noted previously, 5:2–4(1–3) subtly but consistently downplays the role of the kingly figure to stress Yahweh as the King. … the royal figure gains no prestige as king. Rather, whatever he does reflects the presence of Yahweh through Yahweh’s name. … The classic expression of this idea appears in Deut 12:5 … Conceptualizing the temple as the place where Yahweh chose to put his name gave more prominence to the conceptualization of Yahweh dwelling in the heavens.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:4 reflects Deuteronomic name-theology (Deut 12:5; temple as place of the Name vs kābōd/ark presence); the royal figure is subordinate—prestige belongs to Yahweh’s name/presence.

### C-E-17 — 5:3 not to be excised as secondary insertion
- **Locus:** local 68 ≈ raw 3308
- **Quote:** “A significant number of commentators treat 5:4(3) as the original continuation of 5:2(1), arguing that the reference to the action of Yahweh in 5:3(2) interrupts the description of the ruler, and thus represents a secondary insertion. While this is true, that observation does not necessitate the assumption that 5:3 comes from a different hand. … Apart from 5:3 one would have to go all the way back to 4:10 to find another text that could account for the dispersal of Yahweh’s people outside Yahweh’s land. It seems unwise, therefore, to remove 5:3 as a later insertion because 5:4b assumes the presence of 5:3.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Though 5:3 interrupts ruler-description, 5:4b presupposes forced departure supplied by Yahweh’s “giving them up” in 5:3; excision is unwise (also 8Ḥev 1 “they will return”).

---

### C-E-18 — Third group: four “and it will be” (wəhāyâ) openings
- **Locus:** local 72–73, 133 ≈ raw 3312–3313, 3373
- **Quote:** “C. AND IT WILL BE (5:5–9[4–8]) … Mic 5:5(4) nevertheless plays an important role as the opening verse of the third group of sayings in Mic 4–5 that all begin with the phrase and it will be, a phrase that represents a single word in Hebrew (wəhāyâ). In addition to 5:5(4), this introductory marker puts the action in the future and appears in 5:7(6), 8(7), 10(9).”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Mic 5:5–9 (extending into 5:10’s intro) forms the third structural group of chs. 4–5, marked by four wəhāyâ openings (5:5, 7, 8, 10) that future-orient the action.

### C-E-19 — 5:5a transitional: “this will be peace” and compiler’s join
- **Locus:** local 135 ≈ raw 3375
- **Quote:** “unless one interprets the pronoun (zeh) proleptically as an introduction to what follows (‘And this will be peace’), the masculine singular pronoun must refer to the ruler who is the subject of 5:2–4(1–3). … 5:5a(4a) serves a transitional function that probably stems from the compiler who joined the sayings of chapters 4–5 together: it summarizes 5:2–4(1–3), but it begins like 5:7(6), 8(7), 10(9).”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:5a is transitional/compilerial: summarizes the ruler unit while opening like the third group; zeh may proleptically introduce “peace” or (cumbersomely) equate the ruler with peace; MT atnach separates “peace” from “Assyria.”

### C-E-20 — Assyria condition; seven shepherds and eight leaders
- **Locus:** local 136–137 ≈ raw 3376–3377
- **Quote:** “This clause states a condition, formulated as a threat from Assyria (though he enters our land and though he treads upon our citadels) that the informed reader knows will happen. This condition, however, is undercut by the following affirmation: we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight leaders of men. This numerical saying can be interpreted in one of two ways. … as an indefinite number, a more figurative means of saying ‘several’ … but a second way … the second number actually coincides with the number of elements listed…”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:5b states Assyrian invasion as real condition countered by raising “seven shepherds and eight leaders”; numerical chain may mean “several” (Amos-style) or count-matching second number (Prov 30 pattern).

### C-E-21 — Eight kings from Hezekiah to Zedekiah (preferred numerical reading)
- **Locus:** local 156 ≈ raw 3396
- **Quote:** “Interpreted in this manner, the numerical statement in 5:5(4) (we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight leaders of men against him) would recognize the parallel terms, shepherds and leaders, as synonyms, meaning that 5:5(4) should be read as a pronouncement that eight kings will shepherd the people. Read as a prediction of what will happen from the time of Hezekiah’s reign (cf. Mic 1:1) when Assyria laid siege to Jerusalem, eight kings ruled Judah before the temple and the city were destroyed in 587 BCE: Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Preferable reading: seven/eight = eight synonymous shepherds/leaders = the eight Davidic kings from Hezekiah through Zedekiah spanning Assyrian threat to 587 destruction.

### C-E-22 — 5:6: shepherds with sword/dagger against Assyria and land of Nimrod
- **Locus:** local 158–169 ≈ raw 3398–3409
- **Quote:** “Rather than the staff, which can be used to guide and defend the flock, the shepherd in 5:6(5) utilizes a sword and a dagger. Consequently, 5:6(5) depicts hostile action of the shepherd directed against the land of Assyria. … The use of Nimrod to parallel Assyria implies the broader Mesopotamian region in general. The Table of Nations in Gen 10:8–11 describes Nimrod as the son of Cush whose kingdom began with Babylon before he created Nineveh. … Mic 5:6(5) extends the threat of foreign incursion beyond the time of Assyrian hegemony to evoke the threat of Babylon as well. … This portrait comports well with the portrait of Judah’s history from the time of Hezekiah until the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:6’s shepherds act with sword/dagger against Assyria and “land of Nimrod” (Gen 10:8–11 → broader Mesopotamia including Babylon); long-view of Judah’s shepherds vs. imperial threat from Hezekiah to 587; deliverance without unscathed escape; then subject shifts to [[remnant|remnant]] of Jacob.

### C-E-23 — Remnant of Jacob polyvalent; diaspora among many peoples (5:7–8)
- **Locus:** local 170–175 ≈ raw 3410–3415
- **Quote:** “The term remnant should be treated as a polyvalent word. On the one hand, it connotes a promise that implies some will survive. On the other hand, the term implies some will die. … Both verses depict the future remnant of Jacob living outside the land and stress that the remnant is widely scattered. This language thus refers to diaspora populations, but the term remnant of Jacob also draws them together as part of the family. … It also expands the promise to those who were scattered by Assyria and Babylon, to those exiled from Israel as well as Judah.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** “Remnant of Jacob” is polyvalent (survival + death implied); 5:7–8 place the remnant among many peoples/nations as diaspora, still familial via Jacob’s twelve sons; promise expands to Israelite and Judean exiles under Assyria and Babylon.

### C-E-24 — Dew/showers vs lion: fertility and terrifying power
- **Locus:** local 176–178 ≈ raw 3416–3418
- **Quote:** “Micah 5:7(6) depicts the numerical fertility of the remnant by comparing the remnant to the abundant dew that feeds the grass, while 5:8(7) focuses upon the terrifying power of the remnant using the metaphor of a lion capable of terrorizing the sheep. Micah 5:7(6) describes a healthy, fertile people using images of vitality: the dew/showers from Yahweh that do not depend upon human actions. Micah 5:8(7) portrays the future remnant of Zion as a fearsome lion that travels where it will and can attack violently if it so chooses.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Paired metaphors: 5:7 = dew/abundant showers from Yahweh (fertility, independence from human agency); 5:8 = lion among sheep (power to trample/tear without deliverance)—promissory future remnant numerous and powerful.

### C-E-25 — 5:9 transitional: 2ms you; cut off anticipates 5:10–15
- **Locus:** local 180–182 ≈ raw 3420–3422
- **Quote:** “Micah 5:9(8) reads like a transitional verse between the third and fourth group. … returns to the second-person masculine singular address. … Read with 5:8(7), the you in 5:9(8) articulates a scenario in which the nation (like the lion) will act against its enemies. … it also anticipates the recurring Leitwort for the concluding unit (5:10–15[9–14]) where the hiphil perfect first-person common singular form of the same verb (hikrattî) appears … one can also interpret 5:9(8) as a prayer to Yahweh affirming that Yahweh will remove the enemies from the land. This ambiguity is very much in keeping with the transitional function of the verse.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:9 is transitional (like 4:8; 5:2): 2ms “you” may be the nation-as-lion against adversaries, or a prayer that Yahweh cut off enemies; yikkārētû anticipates hikrattî Leitwort of 5:10–13; ABBA parallelism (raise hand / adversaries // enemies / cut off).

---

### C-E-26 — Fourth group: overloaded intro “on that day I will cut off”
- **Locus:** local 188–222 ≈ raw 3428–3462
- **Quote:** “The fourth and final group of sayings (5:10–15[9–14]) begins with a series of formulaic elements. Micah 5:10(9) overloads the introductory clauses with the formulas of the previous group, and it will be (wəhāyâ) and the eschatological day sayings that began the first group in chapter 4 (on that day, cf. 4:6), followed by the hiphil perfect first-person common singular form (wəhikrattî) … The overloaded introduction suggests that the elements comprising 5:10aα(9aα) were deliberately constructed for the context to introduce the following verses.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:10–15 is the fourth group; 5:10aα deliberately overloads wəhāyâ + “on that day” (cf. 4:6) + utterance of Yahweh + hikrattî to adapt preexisting material to context; hikrattî then leads 5:10–13.

### C-E-27 — Original target own people; final form against nations
- **Locus:** local 222, 234–235 ≈ raw 3462, 3474–3475
- **Quote:** “These distinctions suggest that 5:10aβ–13(9aβ–12) existed independently, and that it was adapted to fit the context. … These elements suggest that 5:10aβ–13(9aβ–12) originally served as a pronouncement against Yahweh’s own people, while the editor who brought this composition into its current location has done so with the purpose of condemning foreign nations who will act against Judah. … quite a number of scholars have suggested that the core of this unit originally pronounced judgment against Yahweh’s own people, but these sayings were reformulated in the editorial frame of 5:9–10(8–9), 15(14) as judgments against the nations who will attack Judah. In their final form, the compiler of chapters 4–5 included these pronouncements as punishment of the worship of idols for the nations. This idea represents a significant theological development in postexilic Judah.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Core 5:10aβ–13 originally judged Yahweh’s own people (military power, cities, sorcery, idols); editorial frame (5:9–10, 15) reorients it against hostile nations—postexilic theological development of punishing nations’ idolatry.

### C-E-28 — Content of cut-offs: horses, chariots, cities, fortifications
- **Locus:** local 224–226 ≈ raw 3464–3466
- **Quote:** “Following the introduction, 5:10(9) announces the destruction of the power to wage war with the elimination of the horses and chariots. These elements constitute military weaponry, not a typical means of locomotion. … Without the ability to attack using horses and chariots, the cities will be vulnerable. The two halves of this verse pronounce Yahweh’s devastation upon the cities and fortifications.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:10 removes war-power (horses/chariots as weaponry); 5:11 throws down cities and fortifications, leaving no defense.

### C-E-29 — Sorcery, soothsayers, idols, pillars, Asherim (5:12–14)
- **Locus:** local 228–232 ≈ raw 3468–3472
- **Quote:** “The word sorcery appears only twelve times in the Old Testament. … these references either appear in lists of inappropriate behavior or are associated with the religious practice of Assyria (Nah 3:4) or Babylon (Isa 47:9, 12; Jer 27:9; Dan 2:2). … One may infer … that the practice of sorcery was associated with the worship of foreign deities … The word translated here as soothsayers is actually a participial form from the denominative verb ʿnn, which derives from the noun ‘cloud.’ … This verse condemns the worship of idols. … The pillars refer to stone monuments that represent other deities. … In 5:14(13), the plural form eliminates a direct reference to the deity. Instead, your Asherim may refer to poles used to represent the tree of life that serve as the focal point of worship condemned by the worshipers of Yahweh only.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:12–14 polemicize sorcery (Mesopotamian-associated), soothsaying (possibly cloud-omen diviners), idols, maṣṣēbôt pillars, and plural Asherim (cult poles, not the goddess as such)—practices that typically signal Israel/Judah’s adoption of foreign worship.

### C-E-30 — 5:15: vengeance on nations who did not listen; frame vs core
- **Locus:** local 236 ≈ raw 3476
- **Quote:** “The concluding verse of chapters 4–5 offers a final comment upon the preceding verses, in the process interpreting 5:9(8), 10–14(9–13) as the pronouncements of judgment upon the nations who will attack Judah in the future. Micah 5:15(14) defines the judgment against the enemies as divine judgment by claiming that the nations who did not listen provoked Yahweh’s anger. While most of 5:10–15(9–14) reads like an announcement of judgment against Judah because of its syncretistic practices, the framing verses (5:9[8], 10[9], 15[14]) clearly interpret the action as directed against the nations.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:15 frames the unit as Yahweh’s anger/vengeance on nations that “did not listen”; frames override the surface syncretism-judgment-against-Judah feel of the core.

### C-E-31 — Four groups, four themes; chronological journey structure
- **Locus:** local 238 ≈ raw 3478
- **Quote:** “The four groups of texts that comprise Mic 4–5 (4:1–7; 4:8–5:4[3]; 5:5–9[4–8]; 5:10–15[9–14]) intertwine lexically, but they also focus upon four recurring themes as they portray the future: the changing role of the nations, the fate of Zion, the reaffirmation of Davidic leadership, and the nature of the remnant community. The opening unit (4:1–7) describes life in the distant future (the end of days in Mic 4:1), while the remaining groups back up and explore the journey of how Jerusalem and the nations will get there.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Mic 4–5 = four groups with four recurring themes (nations, Zion, Davidic leadership, remnant); 4:1–7 = end-game (“end of days”); groups 2–4 back up to narrate the journey there.

### C-E-32 — Group-by-group chronological program (now / it will be / on that day)
- **Locus:** local 238 ≈ raw 3478
- **Quote:** “The second group (4:8–5:4[3]) changes the chronological focus to that of the current generation that is threatened in the time of Hezekiah to refer to the time of the prophet based upon 1:1 (e.g., the use of now in 4:9, 10, 11, 14). … The third group (5:5–9[4–8]) promises peace in the coming time (and it will be), a peace that will outlast the Assyrian threat, even though only a remnant of Judah will survive. … The fourth group (5:10–15[9–14]) culminates in a promise to cut off the nations who have not yet learned to listen to Yahweh (5:15[14]). … The ability of the nations to wage war will be cut off (5:10[9]) … thus preparing the ground for the nations’ ability to recognize Yahweh as king, or face retribution from Yahweh himself.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Chronological markers structure reading: group 1 = end of days / on that day; group 2 = “now” (Hezekiah/prophet’s time per 1:1: distress, exile to Babylon, nations, Davidic continuance 5:2–4); group 3 = “and it will be” (Assyrian long struggle + remnant among nations); group 4 = cut off war/idols of non-listening nations, preparing recognition of Yahweh as king (compatibility with 4:1–7 peace vision).

### C-E-33 — Excursus: deliberate postexilic compilation; reading via chronological markers
- **Locus:** local 240–242 ≈ raw 3480–3482
- **Quote:** “EXCURSUS: THE NATURE OF MICAH 4–5 AS COMPILATION … Micah 4–5 combines independent units that explore diverse themes, yet the arrangement of the units demonstrates signs of deliberate editorial cohesion … The key, as has been noted, lies in the frequent vacillation of the chronological markers and the assumption of a reading perspective at the end of the eighth century BCE, the time of the prophet for whom the book is named. While not disputing the scholarly consensus that the compilation of the chapters as well as the dates of composition for the units that comprise chapters 4–5 takes place in the postexilic period, simply dating the oracles and their collection obscures the fact that the collection asks the reader, through clear textual signals, to project the message into the future (4:1, 6; 5:5–9[4–8], 10[9]), as well as to relate the events to now (4:9, 10, 11; 5:1 [4:14]).”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Chs. 4–5 are a deliberate postexilic compilation of independent units with editorial cohesion; proper reading follows chronological markers—future projection (4:1, 6; 5:5–9, 10) and “now” (4:9–11; 5:1)—from an eighth-century prophetic reading stance, not mere dating labels.

### C-E-34 — Interpretive theological function of the compilation
- **Locus:** local 242 ≈ raw 3482
- **Quote:** “In so doing, the chapters take on an interpretive theological function: to provide both explanations for Jerusalem’s ‘coming’ destruction and for the purposeful reconstitution of life with Yahweh as a remnant community that has endured its punishment.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Mic 4–5’s theological function = explain Jerusalem’s (narratively “coming”) destruction and purposeful reconstitution as a remnant community with Yahweh after enduring punishment.

### C-E-35 — Scribal curriculum context; midpoint of the Book of the Twelve
- **Locus:** local 244 ≈ raw 3484
- **Quote:** “Recently, scholars like Odil Steck, Karl van der Toorn, and David Carr have suggested ways that the scribal culture of Judah both shaped and was shaped by an educational system that produced and transmitted its own curriculum in the postexilic period. … In Mic 4–5, the intertwining of motifs, the location of these chapters at the exact middle of the Book of the Twelve, and the way that these chapters interpret the epoch from Hezekiah forward suggest that their compilation played a key role in the developing sense of the importance of prophetic literature for teaching the ways of Yahweh over the span of history that ran from the eighth century BCE to the Persian period.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Compilation plausibly belongs to postexilic scribal-educational culture (Steck, van der Toorn, Carr); Motif-intertwining + midpoint of the [[book-of-the-twelve|Book of the Twelve]] + Hezekiah-to-Persian epoch reading show prophetic literature teaching Yahweh’s ways across history.

### C-E-36 — Textual notes: dagger emendation; peace/Assyria division; LXX variants (select)
- **Locus:** local 111–127, 135 ≈ raw 3351–3367, 3375
- **Quote:** “MT reads ‘with its entrances’ (biptāḥêhā), likely due to accidental transposition. The assumption here of bappətîḥâ (with a dagger) involves the early transposition of two letters … though it is a much less common word, appearing elsewhere only in Ps 55:22. … most English translations seek ways to include Assyria with the word peace … Yet, following this line of interpretation requires questioning why the MT does not combine these two words. The translation used here attempts, instead, to do justice to the MT by keeping 5:5a(4a) syntactically separate from 5:5b(4b).”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Textual decisions: 5:6 “dagger” via early letter transposition vs MT “entrances”; 5:5 MT keeps “this will be peace” separate from “Assyria” (contra many English “peace with/of Assyria”); various LXX/8Ḥev 1/Mur 88 variants noted for shepherds, remnant, lion preposition, etc.

### C-E-37 — Syntactic problems at group seams likely editorial
- **Locus:** local 133 ≈ raw 3373
- **Quote:** “Syntactically, the first and last of these introductions create problems that likely arose from an editorial decision to add wəhāyâ statements in 5:5(4) and 5:10(9) when this preexisting unit was incorporated into its current context.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Awkward syntax at first and last wəhāyâ introductions (5:5; 5:10) likely from editorial addition of those markers when incorporating preexisting material.

### C-E-38 — Compatibility of 5:10–15 with 4:1–7 nations vision
- **Locus:** local 236–238 ≈ raw 3476–3478
- **Quote:** “The pronouncement of the punishment of the nations hostile to Yahweh appears at first glance to run counter to the message of the opening unit of this larger block since 4:1–7 opened with a much more positive message toward the nations in which war ceased (4:3) because the nations submitted themselves to Yahweh’s reign. Yet, the two units are not as incompatible as they seem at first glance. … The punishment also includes the elimination of sorcery and idolatry (5:12–14[11–13]), thus preparing the ground for the nations’ ability to recognize Yahweh as king, or face retribution from Yahweh himself.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Judgment on non-listening nations (5:15) is not incompatible with 4:1–7 peace: cutting off war capacity and idolatry prepares either recognition of Yahweh as king or divine retribution—path to the “end of days” vision.
